```{julia}
cd(@__DIR__)
using Pkg
Pkg.activate(".")
Pkg.instantiate()

```

There is a package called `Turing.jl` that is a powerful tool for Bayesian inference in Julia. It allows you to define probabilistic models and perform inference using various algorithms. Compared to the R/Stan ecosystem, Julia + Turing has both upsides and downside. The main upside is that it allows to use both discrete and continuous distributions. Since the treatment of phylogenetic uncertainty requires marginalization over discrete entitites, this is a big plus. Another upside is that everything is written in one language, Julia, so you avoid the headache to come to grips with Stan. One of the downsides is that there are no off-the-shelf techniques for model comparison, so we will have to either implement them ourselves or to use the RCall interface to R.

We start with loading the necessary packages.

```{julia}
using Turing
using StatsPlots
using Distributions
using DataFrames
using CSV
using LinearAlgebra
using Pigeons
using Glob
using Phylo
using Pipe
using StatsFuns
using ProgressMeter
using Random
```


Now we load the data.

**Edge tree distribution**

```{julia}
# Create data directory if it doesn't exist
isdir("../data") || mkpath("../data")

# Paths
tgz_url = "https://github.com/rbouckaert/global-language-tree-pipeline/releases/download/v1.0.0/all_trees.tgz"
tgz_file = "../data/all_trees.tgz"
tar_file = "../data/all_trees.tar"
tree_dir = "../data/all_trees/"

# Download and extract
if !isdir(tree_dir)
    Downloads.download(tgz_url, tgz_file)

    # Decompress .tgz to .tar
    open(tgz_file) do f_in
        open(tar_file, "w") do f_out
            write(f_out, transcode(GzipDecompressor, read(f_in)))
        end
    end

    # Extract .tar archive
    Tar.extract(tar_file, tree_dir)
    # Move all files from ../data/all_trees/all_trees to ../data/all_trees
    inner_dir = joinpath(tree_dir, "all_trees")
    if isdir(inner_dir)
        for f in readdir(inner_dir; join=true)
            mv(f, joinpath(tree_dir, basename(f)); force=true)
        end
        rm(inner_dir; force=true, recursive=true)
    end
    # Clean up
    rm(tgz_file)
    rm(tar_file)
end


# Load all Newick trees
tree_files = glob("*.tree", tree_dir)

trees = [parsenewick(read(f, String)) for f in tree_files]

# Optionally strip suffixes
for tree in trees
    for tip in getleaves(tree)
        tip.name = split(tip.name, "_")[1]
    end
end

```


**Grambank data**


```{julia}
#| vscode: {languageId: julia}
Random.seed!(1234)  # Set seed for reproducibility
d = @pipe CSV.File("../data/grambank_vals_pruned.csv") |>
          DataFrame |>
          _[rand(1:nrow(_), 20), :] |>
          sort(_, :Language_ID)
taxa = d.Language_ID
```


Now we prune the trees to only include the languages in the data.

```{julia}
#| vscode: {languageId: julia}
pruned_trees = [deepcopy(t) for t in rand(trees, 50)]
for t in pruned_trees
    droptips!(t, setdiff(getleafnames(t), taxa))
end
```

Let us add a combined character `z` to the data, which is $2x+y-1$. 


To illustrate the advantage of the Julia + Turing approach, I implemented the likelihood function for the joint model according to Pagel & Meade (2006) in Julia. The function `get_ll` computes the log-likelihood of the data given a tree and a rate matrix $Q$. The function `decompose_tree` is used to extract the necessary information from the tree structure.


First we create the new character `z` in the data frame `d` that captures the possible combination states of the two characters `x` and `y`. The new character is defined as $z = 2x + y - 1$.


```{julia}
#| vscode: {languageId: julia}
#| output: false

d = @pipe d |> transform(_, [:x, :y] => ByRow((x, y) -> 2x + y + 1) => :z)

```

Then we add the likelihood function `get_ll` as a function of a tree `tree`, a rate matrix `Q`, tip labels `taxa`, and a vector `z` of states for the tip labels. The function `decompose_tree` is a helper function that extracts the necessary information from the tree structure.
```{julia}

function decompose_tree(
    tree::RootedTree
)::@NamedTuple{root::String, mothers::Vector{String}, daughters::Vector{String}, lengths::Vector{Float64}, nodes_dict::Dict{String,Int64}}
    root = getroot(tree).name
    mothers = String[]
    daughters = String[]
    lengths = Float64[]
    for nd in traversal(tree, postorder)
        if !isroot(tree, nd)
            mother = getparent(tree, nd)
            br = getinbound(tree, nd)
            bl = getlength(tree, br)
            push!(mothers, mother.name)
            push!(daughters, nd.name)
            push!(lengths, bl)
        end
    end

    nodes = sort!(unique(vcat(mothers, daughters)))
    nodes_dict = Dict{String,Int}(nodes .=> 1:length(nodes))
    (root=root, mothers=mothers, daughters=daughters, lengths=lengths, nodes_dict=nodes_dict)
end


function get_P(
    t::Float64,
    Q::AbstractMatrix{Float64},
)::Matrix{Float64}
    exp(Q * t)
end

function rates_to_matrix(rates::Vector{Float64})
    Q = zeros(Float64, 4, 4)
    counter = 1
    for i in 1:4, j in 1:4
        if i != j
            Q[i, j] = min(rates[counter], 1e10)
            counter += 1
        end
    end
    for i in 1:4
        Q[i, i] = -sum(Q[i, :])
    end
    return Q
end


function get_ll(
    tree::RootedTree,
    Q::AbstractMatrix;
    taxa=d.Language_ID,
    z::Vector{Int}=d.z
)::Float64
    eq = get_P(1000.0, Q)[:, 1]
    root, mothers, daughters, lengths, nodes_dict = decompose_tree(tree)
    ll = zeros(Float64, length(nodes_dict), maximum(z))
    for (l, s) in zip(taxa, z)
        ll[nodes_dict[l], :] .= -Inf
        ll[nodes_dict[l], s] = 0.0
    end
    @views for i in eachindex(lengths)
        dgt = nodes_dict[daughters[i]]
        mth = nodes_dict[mothers[i]]
        P = get_P(lengths[i], Q)
        tmp = log.(P) .+ ll[dgt, :]'
        for j in 1:size(tmp, 1)
            ll[mth, j] += logsumexp(view(tmp, j, :))
        end
    end
    logsumexp(ll[nodes_dict[root], :] + log.(eq))
end
```

Let us test whether the likelihood function works correctly.

```{julia}
@showprogress for _ in 1:10000
    rates = exp.(rand(Normal(0, 1), 12))
    Q = rates_to_matrix(rates)
    tree = rand(pruned_trees)
    get_ll(tree, Q; taxa=taxa, z=d.z)
end

```


Now we create a Turing model using this likelihood function. The model will have a prior on the rate matrix $Q$ and will use the `get_ll` function to compute the log-likelihood of the data given the tree and the rate matrix.

```{julia}


@model function bayes_model(pruned_trees, taxa, z)
    urates ~ filldist(Normal(0.0, 1.0), 12)
    rates = exp.(urates)  # lognormal prior
    Q = rates_to_matrix(rates)

    latent_index ~ Normal(0.0, 1.0)
    n = length(pruned_trees)
    tree_index = clamp(Int(ceil(cdf(Normal(0.0, 1.0), latent_index) * n)), 1, n)

    tree = pruned_trees[tree_index]

    ll = get_ll(tree, Q; taxa=taxa, z=z)
    Turing.@addlogprob! ll
    return vcat(rates, [tree_index])
end

```



This model defines a prior on the rates using an exponential distribution, constructs the rate matrix $Q$ from the rates, and computes the log-likelihood of the data given the tree and the rate matrix using the `get_ll` function. The model can then be used for Bayesian inference using Turing's sampling algorithms.

The main difference from the R/Stan approach is that we can simultaneously sample from the tree space and the rate space, which is not possible in Stan. In Stan, you would have to compute the likelihood for all trees in the tree sample in each sampling step, which is computationally expensive. In Julia + Turing, we can sample from the tree space and the rate space simultaneously, which is much more efficient.


```{julia}
model = bayes_model(pruned_trees, taxa, d.z)

```

We can now sample from the model using the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm with MCMCThreads. This will allow us to sample from the posterior distribution of the rates and the tree index.

```{julia}

chain = sample(
    model,
    MH(),
    MCMCThreads(),
    20_000,
    4,
    progress=true
)

```


```{julia}
struct CTMCdependent
    trees::Vector{RootedTree}
    taxa::Vector{String}
    z::Vector{Int}
    posterior::Bool
end

function (ctmc_dependent::CTMCdependent)(pars)
    ndim = length(pars)
    ll = logpdf(MvNormal(zeros(ndim), ones(ndim)), pars)
    if ctmc_dependent.posterior
        urates = pars[1:(end-1)]
        rates = exp.(urates)
        Q = rates_to_matrix(rates)
        latent_index = pars[end]
        n = length(ctmc_dependent.trees)
        tree_index = clamp(Int(ceil(cdf(Normal(0.0, 1.0), latent_index) * n)), 1, n)
        tree = ctmc_dependent.trees[tree_index]
        ll += get_ll(tree, Q; taxa=ctmc_dependent.taxa, z=ctmc_dependent.z)
    end
    return ll
end

```


```{julia}
ctmc_dependent = CTMCdependent(pruned_trees, taxa, d.z, true)

ctmc_dependent(zeros(13))

```

```{julia}

Pigeons.initialization(::CTMCdependent, ::AbstractRNG, ::Int) = zeros(13)
pt = pigeons(
        target = CTMCdependent(pruned_trees, taxa, d.z, true),
        reference =  CTMCdependent(pruned_trees, taxa, d.z, false),
        multithreaded = true,
        record = [traces; record_default()]
    )

```
